solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, mirror symmetry); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Where executives fly shown by company form

parts.note: a company is a business, a firm
a form at school is a class

explanation.surface: Something about corporate travel is revealed by a company document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' reads as paperwork, but it is the school sense: a year group or class.
explanation.definitionFit: The premium cabin on airliners between economy and first is where travelling managers are typically seated.

clue.text: Harsh noise from pub, King's Head

parts.note: a bar is a pub or a room in one

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here of King's

explanation.surface: A rough sound comes from a pub called the King's Head.
explanation.walkthrough: The King's Head reads as a pub name; instead 'Head' takes the first letter of King's.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's short gruff cry, or any curt rough shout, is a harsh noise.

clue.text: More cheeky son, silly? That is right

parts.note: S is the genealogical abbreviation for son
a silly person is an ass
i.e. (id est) means that is

explanation.surface: A parent wonders whether a son is being more cheeky or just silly.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassy is an informal synonym for cheeky or impudent, and this is its comparative form.

clue.text: Too trusting, don't insist on getting name for whiskey

indicators.note: getting one letter for another signals a swap, the name letter taking the whiskey letter's place

parts.note: to waive a right or demand is not to insist on it
Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone gullible lets a whiskey demand drop.
explanation.walkthrough: WAIVE, with its W (whiskey, the NATO code word) replaced by N for name.
explanation.definitionFit: A naive person is innocent and credulous, inclined to believe others too readily.

clue.text: Stole small cleaning cloth — shamed finally

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a wipe is a disposable cleaning cloth

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of shamed

explanation.surface: A thief pocketed a small cloth and ended up disgraced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' could be a noun, a scarf, beside 'cloth', but it is the past tense of steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Swiped is a colloquial past tense for stealing, as in snatching something quickly.

clue.text: Not half common writing instruments a politician provided as replacement

indicators.note: taking not half of common means keeping only its first half

parts.note: pens are instruments for writing
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Ordinary pens and a politician are offered as a substitute for something lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' cuts common to its first half, COM. A Tory is a British Conservative.
explanation.definitionFit: Compensatory payments or measures make good a loss, standing in for what was taken.

clue.text: A Buddhist regularly missing inspection

indicators.note: regularly missing letters of Buddhist means every other letter is dropped, keeping the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th

explanation.surface: A Buddhist is often absent when the inspection takes place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly missing' drops B, D, H and S from Buddhist, leaving UDIT.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is a formal official examination, typically of accounts or procedures.

clue.text: Rebel mob wants restyled military wear

indicators.note: restyled means given a new style, so the letters of the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rioting crowd demands a new look in army clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: This officer's belt with a diagonal shoulder strap is a classic item of army uniform, named after General Sam Browne.

clue.text: Somewhat cross, I niggle composer

indicators.note: Somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A slightly irritated person admits to nagging a composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Gioachino Rossini was an Italian composer of operas such as The Barber of Seville.

clue.text: Fashion initially marvellous computer device

parts.note: a mode is a fashion or style

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of marvellous

explanation.surface: A trendy, marvellous gadget for a computer.
explanation.definitionFit: A modem is hardware that links a computer to a network by modulating signals.

clue.text: Unusual term one cited for life-saver?

indicators.note: unusual suggests the letters of these three words appear in an odd new order

explanation.surface: An odd phrase is quoted as describing someone who rescues people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'life-saver' suggests a lifeguard; the question mark admits the answer saves lives in a less obvious way.
explanation.definitionFit: By locating buried explosives, this sweeping device prevents deaths, so it saves lives, by example.

clue.text: Get together, being clever, to get around flipping mess?

indicators.note: to get around means one word is wrapped round the other

parts.note: a clever person is able

indicators.note: flipping means the word mess is turned over, read backwards

explanation.surface: A clever person wonders how to avoid a flipping mess when meeting up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild British curse, but here it is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble is to gather or congregate, as a group of people meeting in one place.

clue.text: Type stocking extremely bizarre water ice

indicators.note: stocking means holding within, so one part is placed inside the other

parts.note: a sort is a type or kind

indicators.note: extremely takes the extreme letters, first and last, of bizarre

explanation.surface: A shop sells a very odd kind of water ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stocking' looks like hosiery, but here it means holding something inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorbet is a frozen dessert of fruit juice and sugar, also called water ice.

clue.text: Following old routine, lady drops a daughter off? Precisely

parts.note: ex means former, old
a comedian's routine is an act

indicators.note: drops ... off says these letters are taken out of the word lady

explanation.surface: Following an old dance routine, a woman lets her daughter go home.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady loses A and D (daughter), leaving LY, which follows EXACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Exactly and precisely are synonyms, both meaning accurately or in every detail.

clue.text: European Society boast reveals money held by third party

parts.note: to crow is to boast

explanation.surface: A European club's bragging exposes funds held in trust.
explanation.definitionFit: Escrow is a legal arrangement where an independent agent keeps funds until a deal completes.

clue.text: Met ruin working out duration of program

indicators.note: working out a puzzle means rearranging its pieces, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone met disaster while calculating how long software runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Run time is the period during which software is executing, so its duration.

clue.text: Just starting maybe you really treasure lovely evergreen shrub

indicators.note: just starting means only the starting letters of each of the following words are used

explanation.surface: A gardener says you may well treasure a lovely evergreen bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evergreen shrub' reads as the definition, but evergreen supplies the final E and only 'shrub' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Myrtle is a fragrant Mediterranean bush with glossy leaves and white flowers.

clue.text: What could give sect, say, great delight?

indicators.note: could give suggests the letters of sect and say may be rearranged to produce something new

explanation.surface: A question about what would delight a religious group.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecstasy is an overwhelming feeling of joy or rapture, an extreme delight.

clue.text: From outskirts of Swindon, inaccurate informer

indicators.note: the outskirts of a word are its outer letters, the first and last of Swindon

parts.note: an estimate that is out is inaccurate

explanation.surface: A misleading tip-off comes from the edge of Swindon, an English town.
explanation.walkthrough: SNOUT is British slang for a police informer.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a snout is someone who passes tips to the police, an informer.

clue.text: Trace of metal for example recalled

parts.note: tin is a metal

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: e.g. is short for exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A sample of metal is remembered as a hint.
explanation.definitionFit: A tinge is a slight trace or hint, as of colour or feeling.

clue.text: Encourage sounds of disapproval? Terrible at first

parts.note: boos are jeers of disapproval

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of Terrible

explanation.surface: A performer asks whether jeers count as encouragement when things start badly.
explanation.definitionFit: To boost someone is to encourage them or raise their spirits.

clue.text: Time outsiders avoid herring, English dish

indicators.note: the outsiders of herring, its first and last letters, are avoided, keeping the middle

explanation.surface: It is time to skip herring and serve an English dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrine is a pâté-like dish of meat or fish cooked and served in a mould.

clue.text: Aristocracy, no longer grand, feel reduced cost of admission

indicators.note: no longer grand means the letter for grand is dropped

parts.note: the gentry are the upper classes, close to aristocracy
G is the abbreviation for grand, a thousand pounds

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, so feel loses its last letter

explanation.surface: The upper classes, no longer rich, feel the price of entry is lower.
explanation.walkthrough: GENTRY loses G (grand) to give ENTRY; feel loses its end to give FEE.
explanation.definitionFit: An entry fee is the charge paid for being admitted to an event or place.

clue.text: Opening contest shunned by beginner

indicators.note: shunned by its beginner means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: an event is a contest in a sports programme

explanation.surface: A novice avoids the opening race of the competition.
explanation.definitionFit: A vent is an aperture or outlet through which air or gas escapes.
